newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - New share software hides trail, cuts cost.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - New share software hides trail, cuts cost.

text.p: New share information software for Britain's investment community, could cut trading costs and conceal an investor's dealing intentions until the last moment, according to the chairman of a group promoting the new programme.

The London-based Financial Information Exchange Group (FIX) -- a group of market representatives -- says the system, which has already taken hold in the United States, would help to improve market liquidity by making it easier for sellers and buyers to find each other.

"The push for development of the programme came from large institutions who, when dealing, leave behind big footprints. It's going to work, potential users have taken the initiative," said FIX chairman Alan Line.
The system for communication is a computer protocol, a software programme which potential users can currently call up and copy free of charge on the Internet.
"Information, via the protocol (software format), can be disseminated speedily and competitively to allow trading with minimum impact on the equity market," Line told Reuters in a recent interview.
Users would not deal via the programme, but would gain information anonymously about bid and offer prices before making their intentions known by contacting a broker or institution, Line said.
Thereafter, traditional methods of dealing would take over.

Investors and brokers would be able to swap messages using the programme and indications of interest posted by brokers could be be picked up by investors, said Line, who is also director of dealing at Foreign & Colonial Management in London.
The project was started in the United States in 1993 by Salomon Brothers and Fidelity Investments. It went live in 1995 and 150 brokers and 80 institutions are now estimated to be users.

Liquidity or lack of it, often viewed as a major problem by institutions with an ever-increasing number of deals to execute, is expected to be significantly improved as more institutions and brokers come on line.
"With a telephone, there are a limited number of brokers and institutions you can reach. The present system of dissemination of information by fax is less than satisfactory," said Line.
With the protocol, an investor will be able to pinpoint the liquidity very quickly.

In Britain the target is for four institutions and six brokers to use the programme by March, with double the number by the end of the year. Within three years, Line said he expected most investment institutions and brokers to be users.

"The London group was set up last year to promote the protocol globally. We expect the world's mature financial markets and global companies to move quickly to integrate the protocol within their systems once they see the advantages," Line said.
Line said the programme was compatible with any system. Users have the choice of a financial information vendor or the Internet, but the latter may pose a security problem.

"Communicating on the Internet can leave an audit trail that can be hacked into and even your messages can be interfered with. But technology is moving so fast this may not be a problem in a couple of years."
"We believe vendors of financial information have started development work to incorporate the programme into their products," said Line.
Scottish institutions have also given the concept an enthusiastic response, said the FIX chairman.
Current development is in the equity markets but fixed-income and derivative instruments could be included.
"Foreign exchange is already a global and liquid market."
Line is also chairman of the Institutional Dealers' Association, an informal group that aims to provide a discussion forum on issues of structural changes in the financial markets.
